scenes.visual: Title card on black: THE OXYGEN BARGAIN. Beneath it a thin horizontal line slowly fills from rust-orange at the left to clear sky-blue at the right. A single small O2 molecule (two red circles joined by a double bond) drifts across the line and fades. Subtitle in small type: how oxygen arrived, why it is dangerous, and how cells learned to use it.
Movement card, white serif on deep umber: I. A WORLD WITHOUT OXYGEN. It dissolves upward like heat shimmer.

scenes.tts: Picture Earth about three billion years ago. There are oceans, volcanoes and sunlight. But there is almost no oxygen in the air.
scenes.visual: Wide landscape built from layered polygons: a dark basalt plain, low black volcanic cones venting grey plumes, a flat shallow sea in the middle distance. The sky is a gradient from dull ochre at the horizon to brown-grey overhead. A faint pale sun. A time stamp in the corner counts back and settles on ~3 billion years ago.
scenes.narration: Picture Earth about three billion years ago. There are oceans, volcanoes and sunlight. But there is almost no oxygen in the air.

scenes.tts: The sky may have been hazy, perhaps tinted orange by a methane haze. Nobody saw it, so we rebuild it from ancient rocks.
scenes.visual: The camera tilts up into the sky. A soft orange haze layer (semi-transparent band of small dots) thickens, then a large question mark fades in and out over it. A small rock icon labelled 'evidence: ancient rocks' sits at the bottom edge.
scenes.narration: The sky may have been hazy, perhaps tinted orange by a methane haze. Nobody saw it, so we rebuild it from ancient rocks.

scenes.tts: The oceans held dissolved iron, in its reduced, ferrous form. With little oxygen to take its electrons, much of that iron stayed dissolved.
scenes.visual: Cut beneath the sea surface. The water is a murky green-grey and full of small drifting dots labelled Fe2+. Zoom on one: a ferrous iron ion with a single yellow electron dot highlighted at its edge, labelled 'one electron to give'.
scenes.narration: The oceans held dissolved iron, in its reduced, ferrous form. With little oxygen to take its electrons, much of that iron stayed dissolved.

scenes.tts: Life was already here, and all of it was microbial. Cells likely made energy by fermenting or by making methane. Some may have reduced sulfate.
scenes.visual: On the sea floor, a soft carpet of tiny rod and sphere cells in muted purples and browns. Three labelled icons pop up above clusters: 'fermentation', 'methane makers', 'sulfate reducers?' (the last with a small question mark). Small bubbles of CH4 rise from the mud.
scenes.narration: Life was already here, and all of it was microbial. Cells likely made energy by fermenting or by making methane. Some may have reduced sulfate.

scenes.tts: Every one of those lifestyles moves electrons from a donor to an acceptor. Oxygen, a far more powerful acceptor, was scarce.
scenes.visual: Abstract diagram: for each of the three lifestyles a yellow electron dot hops from a donor box on the left to an acceptor box on the right, releasing a small flash. On the far right a large slot labelled O2 with a dashed outline and only a faint trace inside: 'scarce'.
scenes.narration: Every one of those lifestyles moves electrons from a donor to an acceptor. Oxygen, a far more powerful acceptor, was scarce.

scenes.tts: The land had no plants and no animals, though microbes may have crusted damp patches. Plants would not arrive for over two billion years.
scenes.visual: Back to the wide landscape. Slow pan across bare rock and dark sand, acid rain streaking diagonally in thin grey lines. No plants anywhere, but thin dark microbial crusts film a few damp hollows, labelled 'microbial crusts?'. Silence except the plumes drifting.
scenes.narration: The land had no plants and no animals, though microbes may have crusted damp patches. Plants would not arrive for over two billion years.

scenes.visual: Hold on the empty landscape; the plumes drift; the orange sky dims slightly.
Movement card, white on dark teal: II. THE OXYGEN ARRIVES.

scenes.tts: Then came a new trick. Cyanobacteria learned to pull electrons out of water, powered by sunlight. The waste product was oxygen gas.
scenes.visual: Close-up on one cyanobacterial cell, a blue-green rounded rod with stacked internal membranes. Sunlight rays strike it. Two water molecules (2 H2O) enter; four yellow electron dots are pulled out and race along the membranes, four small H+ dots are released, and one O2 molecule pops out the other side as a red pair of circles. Small equation in the corner: 2 H2O → O2 + 4 H+ + 4 e−.
scenes.narration: Then came a new trick. Cyanobacteria learned to pull electrons out of water, powered by sunlight. The waste product was oxygen gas.

scenes.tts: Water holds its electrons tightly. Photosystem two splits it, and photosystem one then boosts the electrons higher. This machinery evolved once, in the ancestors of cyanobacteria. Plants later gained it by taking in a cyanobacterium.
scenes.visual: Split screen: a water molecule gripping its electrons tightly (yellow dots held close by a red oxygen). Two light-catching complexes in a membrane, side by side, each lit by a sunbeam. The first splits water and releases O2; its electrons pass to the second, which gives them a second boost. Labels: 'Photosystem II: splits water' and 'Photosystem I: boosts the electrons'.
scenes.narration: Water holds its electrons tightly. Photosystem two splits it, and photosystem one then boosts the electrons higher. This machinery evolved once, in the ancestors of cyanobacteria. Plants later gained it by taking in a cyanobacterium.

scenes.tts: In shallow seas, these cells spread as glowing, sticky mats. Similar mats still build layered mounds, called stromatolites, in some bays and lakes today.
scenes.visual: Pull back to a shallow, sunlit bay. A cyanobacterial mat spreads across the floor as a glowing blue-green carpet that pulses softly with light. Tiny O2 bubbles stream upward. Cut to a cross-section of a layered dome mound, layers stacking like an onion; label 'stromatolite (living examples today in some bays and lakes, e.g. Shark Bay)'.
scenes.narration: In shallow seas, these cells spread as glowing, sticky mats. Similar mats still build layered mounds, called stromatolites, in some bays and lakes today.

scenes.tts: Predict. If cyanobacteria were releasing oxygen, why did the air not fill with it right away?
scenes.visual: Question card over the bubbling mat: 'If cyanobacteria were releasing oxygen, why did the air not fill with it right away?' The O2 bubbles freeze in place.
scenes.narration: Predict. If cyanobacteria were releasing oxygen, why did the air not fill with it right away?

scenes.visual: The question card stays; the bubbles hang frozen; a slow clock hand sweeps once.

scenes.tts: Because oxygen had many places to go. Dissolved iron handed its electrons to oxygen, formed rust-like minerals, and sank.
scenes.visual: Bubbles resume. Each O2 meets four drifting Fe2+ dots; each iron gives up one yellow electron to the oxygen (four in all), and the irons turn rust-red (Fe3+) and clump into a tiny flake of ferric oxyhydroxide that begins to sink. Small equation: 4 Fe2+ + O2 + 10 H2O → 4 Fe(OH)3 + 8 H+.
scenes.narration: Because oxygen had many places to go. Dissolved iron handed its electrons to oxygen, formed rust-like minerals, and sank.

scenes.visual: The sea-floor view, time-lapsed. Red iron flakes rain down and settle into a thin red stripe; then a grey silica stripe; then red again. A few flakes form beside purple iron-oxidizing microbes in the dim water with no O2 bubbles nearby, tagged 'no oxygen needed?'. The bands stack up, alternating red and silver-grey, until they form a thick striped wall. The camera rises to show a modern cliff face of the same stripes, labelled 'banded iron formation'.

scenes.tts: Layer by layer, iron and silica built banded iron formations. Some layers may record microbes rusting iron without oxygen. Much of the iron we mine today comes from them.
scenes.visual: The striped cliff with a tiny mining truck at its base, for scale.
scenes.narration: Layer by layer, iron and silica built banded iron formations. Some layers may record microbes rusting iron without oxygen. Much of the iron we mine today comes from them.

scenes.tts: Their biggest pulse came just before and as oxygen began to rise.
scenes.visual: A histogram along the timeline: banded iron deposits swell to their largest pulse around 2.6 to 2.4 billion years ago, just before and at the start of the oxygenation band, then thin out, with a few smaller later pulses.
scenes.narration: Their biggest pulse came just before and as oxygen began to rise.

scenes.tts: Iron was not the only sink. Volcanic gases, methane and minerals on land all consumed oxygen too.
scenes.visual: A bar of incoming O2 arrows on the left. It splits into several sinks, each a labelled funnel: 'dissolved iron', 'volcanic gases (H2, H2S, CO)', 'methane', 'rocks on land'. Only a trickle passes through to a gauge labelled 'air'.
scenes.narration: Iron was not the only sink. Volcanic gases, methane and minerals on land all consumed oxygen too.

scenes.tts: Cyanobacteria most likely arose well before oxygen built up, though by how long is debated. Some rocks hint at brief whiffs of oxygen before that lasting rise.
scenes.visual: A geological timeline ribbon from 3.5 to 1.5 billion years. A green bar labelled 'cyanobacterial ancestors (start uncertain)' begins well before 2.5, its left end fuzzy and dashed. A few tiny pale blue puffs flicker on the ribbon before 2.5, after the green bar has begun, labelled 'whiffs?'.
scenes.narration: Cyanobacteria most likely arose well before oxygen built up, though by how long is debated. Some rocks hint at brief whiffs of oxygen before that lasting rise.

scenes.tts: Then, between about two point four and two point one billion years ago, oxygen rose, wavered, and finally stayed. Geologists call this the Great Oxygenation Event.
scenes.visual: On the timeline, a band between 2.4 and 2.1 billion years glows blue and is labelled 'Great Oxygenation Event'. A gauge labelled 'O2 in air' wobbles up and down within the band before settling at a low but lasting level, well below a dashed line marked 'today'. Small note on the gauge: 'schematic; levels uncertain'.
scenes.narration: Then, between about two point four and two point one billion years ago, oxygen rose, wavered, and finally stayed. Geologists call this the Great Oxygenation Event.

scenes.tts: The methane haze may have thinned, leaving a clearer sky. Even so, oxygen stayed far below today's level for a very long time.
scenes.visual: Return to the wide landscape. The orange haze thins and lifts, leaving a clearer sky. Shallow coastal water turns clear teal, but the camera dips to show the deep water below still murky green and oxygen-free, labelled 'deep ocean: still anoxic'. Glowing mats line the shore.
scenes.narration: The methane haze may have thinned, leaving a clearer sky. Even so, oxygen stayed far below today's level for a very long time.

scenes.visual: Hold on the clearer sky over teal shallows and dark depths, mats glowing at the shoreline.

scenes.tts: Was there a mass die-off of anaerobes? It is often said, but the evidence is thin. Anaerobes clearly survived, in mud, deep water and other airless places.
scenes.visual: A headline-style card reads 'Mass die-off of anaerobes?' and a magnifying glass hovers over a fossil strip that shows nothing. Then the camera dives into ancient dark mud and anoxic deep water, each full of busy purple anaerobic cells. A small inset in the corner, labelled 'today', shows a gut-shaped tube.
scenes.narration: Was there a mass die-off of anaerobes? It is often said, but the evidence is thin. Anaerobes clearly survived, in mud, deep water and other airless places.

scenes.tts: They thrive there still, including in your own gut.
scenes.visual: Inside the gut-shaped tube, anaerobic cells fermenting happily; label 'still here: your gut'.
scenes.narration: They thrive there still, including in your own gut.

scenes.tts: Oxygen did not end the old world of life. It pushed it into the shadows.
scenes.visual: The landscape again, now split: bright blue sky and glowing mats above; below the sediment line, a dark band where purple anaerobic cells still teem.
scenes.narration: Oxygen did not end the old world of life. It pushed it into the shadows.

scenes.visual: Movement card, white on deep crimson: III. OXYGEN IS DANGEROUS.

scenes.tts: Why should oxygen be dangerous at all? Oxygen strongly pulls in four electrons, to become water.
scenes.visual: A single O2 molecule fills the frame, two red spheres. Around it four empty electron slots appear, drawn as dashed circles. A caption: 'O2 + 4 e− + 4 H+ → 2 H2O'.
scenes.narration: Why should oxygen be dangerous at all? Oxygen strongly pulls in four electrons, to become water.

scenes.tts: But its two unpaired electrons make it slow to react with most molecules. It tends to take electrons one at a time.
scenes.visual: Two small arrows, both pointing up, sit in the O2 molecule's outer orbitals (the two unpaired electrons). An ordinary molecule offering a matched pair of electrons approaches and is turned away. A metal ion or radical then passes a single electron across. Label: 'spin rule: one electron at a time'.
scenes.narration: But its two unpaired electrons make it slow to react with most molecules. It tends to take electrons one at a time.

scenes.tts: Predict. If oxygen picks up electrons one at a time, what forms along the way?
scenes.visual: Question card: 'If oxygen picks up electrons one at a time, what forms along the way?' Behind it, a staircase of four steps from O2 down to H2O, the middle steps blank.
scenes.narration: Predict. If oxygen picks up electrons one at a time, what forms along the way?

scenes.visual: The staircase stays, middle steps blank; a soft pulse on each blank step.

scenes.tts: Partly reduced oxygen. One electron makes superoxide. Two make hydrogen peroxide. Three make a hydroxyl radical, plus water. That radical attacks almost anything it touches.
scenes.visual: The blank steps fill in as each yellow electron drops onto the staircase, with small H+ dots joining from the side. Step one: a red molecule with a jagged glow, 'superoxide O2•−'. Step two: 'hydrogen peroxide H2O2'. Step three: a violently flickering 'hydroxyl radical •OH' beside a calm 'H2O'. Step four: calm blue '2 H2O'. Header label: 'possible reduction intermediates'.
scenes.narration: Partly reduced oxygen. One electron makes superoxide. Two make hydrogen peroxide. Three make a hydroxyl radical, plus water. That radical attacks almost anything it touches.

scenes.visual: Hold on the staircase; the hydroxyl radical keeps crackling.

scenes.tts: Together these are called reactive oxygen species. They break DNA, damage proteins, and set off chain reactions in membrane lipids.
scenes.visual: Three panels. A DNA double helix with a strand snapping. A folded protein ribbon whose side chains turn orange and unravel. A lipid bilayer where tails kink, a chain reaction ripples sideways, and a hole opens. Label above: 'reactive oxygen species (ROS)'.
scenes.narration: Together these are called reactive oxygen species. They break DNA, damage proteins, and set off chain reactions in membrane lipids.

scenes.tts: Iron makes it worse. Ferrous iron hands an electron to hydrogen peroxide, releasing the hydroxyl radical.
scenes.visual: A ferrous iron dot (Fe2+) meets H2O2. A yellow electron jumps from iron to the peroxide, which splits into a hydroxide ion (OH−) and a crackling •OH that flies off. The iron turns red (Fe3+). Callback flash to the rusting flakes from earlier.
scenes.narration: Iron makes it worse. Ferrous iron hands an electron to hydrogen peroxide, releasing the hydroxyl radical.

scenes.tts: This is one reason cells keep most of their iron tightly bound, much of it stored inside proteins.
scenes.visual: Most iron atoms snap into cage-like ferritin shells (a hollow sphere of subunits holding a mineral core), and some sit in heme rings doing their jobs. A small pool of loose iron dots remains, each held by a small partner molecule.
scenes.narration: This is one reason cells keep most of their iron tightly bound, much of it stored inside proteins.

scenes.tts: Here is the idea that ties this film together. Every way of living with oxygen is a way of handling its electrons.
scenes.visual: Clean black screen. The guiding idea writes on in white, with the word 'electrons' in glowing yellow: 'Every way of living with oxygen is a way of handling its electrons.'
scenes.narration: Here is the idea that ties this film together. Every way of living with oxygen is a way of handling its electrons.

scenes.visual: The guiding idea holds on screen; one yellow electron dot circles it slowly.

scenes.tts: Cells evolved and spread defenses. Superoxide dismutase turns superoxide into hydrogen peroxide. Catalase turns hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
scenes.visual: Two enzyme blobs appear as friendly shapes. 'Superoxide dismutase' grabs two superoxides plus two H+ and releases H2O2 plus O2. 'Catalase' takes two H2O2 and releases two waters and O2. The crackling glows go calm.
scenes.narration: Cells evolved and spread defenses. Superoxide dismutase turns superoxide into hydrogen peroxide. Catalase turns hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.

scenes.tts: Some bacteria went further and put oxygen to work. They placed it at the end of an electron-transport chain.
scenes.visual: A bacterium in cross-section with a chain of protein complexes in its membrane. Yellow electrons tumble down the chain like a waterfall of steps; at the bottom O2 catches them and becomes water. The drop to oxygen is drawn as the largest.
scenes.narration: Some bacteria went further and put oxygen to work. They placed it at the end of an electron-transport chain.

scenes.tts: Oxygen is the strongest common acceptor. So an electron that falls all the way to oxygen releases much more energy.
scenes.visual: An energy ladder: donors high on the left, acceptors lower; sulfate and others sit partway down, O2 at the very bottom. An electron falling to O2 releases a big burst; to sulfate, a small one.
scenes.narration: Oxygen is the strongest common acceptor. So an electron that falls all the way to oxygen releases much more energy.

scenes.tts: Fermenting glucose to lactate or ethanol yields two A T P. Respiring it fully with oxygen, as our cells do, yields around thirty.
scenes.visual: Two stacks of ATP coins: a short stack of two labelled 'fermentation to lactate or ethanol, per glucose' and a tall stack of about thirty labelled 'aerobic respiration in our cells, per glucose'.
scenes.narration: Fermenting glucose to lactate or ethanol yields two A T P. Respiring it fully with oxygen, as our cells do, yields around thirty.

scenes.tts: But the chain is not perfect. A small fraction of electrons slip off early, often at complexes one and three, making superoxide.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the chain, now drawn as Complex I, ubiquinone (Q), Complex III, cytochrome c and Complex IV. Most yellow electrons flow smoothly down to Complex IV, but at Complex I and Complex III an occasional electron sparks off sideways, hits a nearby O2, and makes a red, crackling superoxide. A counter label: 'a small fraction'.
scenes.narration: But the chain is not perfect. A small fraction of electrons slip off early, often at complexes one and three, making superoxide.

scenes.visual: Hold on the leaking chain; a few red sparks flicker beside the steady stream.
Movement card, white on deep violet: IV. A CELL INSIDE A CELL.

scenes.tts: Now move forward, to some time after oxygen rose. The oldest widely accepted eukaryote fossils are more than one and a half billion years old.
scenes.visual: The timeline ribbon returns. The Great Oxygenation Event band glows behind; an arrow slides forward to a broad fuzzy zone after it, labelled 'eukaryotes appear (timing uncertain)'. A small fossil cell icon marks 'oldest widely accepted eukaryote fossils: >1.5 billion years'.
scenes.narration: Now move forward, to some time after oxygen rose. The oldest widely accepted eukaryote fossils are more than one and a half billion years old.

scenes.tts: The host was most likely an archaeon, related to today's Asgard archaea. Whether it already had a nucleus is still debated.
scenes.visual: A large irregular cell with thin, branching protrusions drifts in, coloured soft amber, labelled 'archaeal host (Asgard relative)'. A faint dashed circle where a nucleus might go carries a question mark, labelled 'nucleus yet?'.
scenes.narration: The host was most likely an archaeon, related to today's Asgard archaea. Whether it already had a nucleus is still debated.

scenes.tts: Asgard archaea were first found as DNA in deep sea sediments. Their genomes carry many genes once thought unique to eukaryotes.
scenes.visual: A deep-sea vent field near a dark ridge, with a sediment core pulled upward; DNA sequences stream out of it and assemble into a genome icon labelled 'Asgard archaea'. A few genes light up, labelled 'genes once thought unique to eukaryotes'.
scenes.narration: Asgard archaea were first found as DNA in deep sea sediments. Their genomes carry many genes once thought unique to eukaryotes.

scenes.tts: The guest was a bacterium related to today's alphaproteobacteria. It could probably respire, and may have used oxygen.
scenes.visual: A small pink rod-shaped bacterium with folded inner membranes swims in, labelled 'alphaproteobacterial relative'. Inside it, a tiny version of the electron chain glows.
scenes.narration: The guest was a bacterium related to today's alphaproteobacteria. It could probably respire, and may have used oxygen.

scenes.tts: Somehow, the archaeon came to enclose the bacterium. And instead of being digested, the guest stayed.
scenes.visual: The amber host's protrusions wrap slowly around the pink bacterium, folding over it until it sits inside, enclosed. A small tag reads 'one proposed mechanism'. Its inner chain keeps glowing. The host's outline settles into a single smooth cell with a glowing pink passenger.
scenes.narration: Somehow, the archaeon came to enclose the bacterium. And instead of being digested, the guest stayed.

scenes.visual: Hold on the merged cell; the pink passenger glows and divides once inside the host.

scenes.tts: Gene trees suggest that this happened only once. Every mitochondrion today descends from that single guest.
scenes.visual: A phylogenetic tree: many branches of alphaproteobacteria in pink, one branch leading to a single node labelled 'mitochondria', which then fans out into plants, animals, fungi and protists. Credit line: after Gray, Burger and Lang, 1999.
scenes.narration: Gene trees suggest that this happened only once. Every mitochondrion today descends from that single guest.

scenes.tts: Most mitochondria still show their bacterial past. They have two membranes, their own DNA, bacteria-like ribosomes, and they divide by pinching in two.
scenes.visual: A typical mitochondrion beside a free bacterium, with matching features ticked off in pairs: two membranes, their own DNA, ribosomes of bacterial ancestry, division by pinching in two.
scenes.narration: Most mitochondria still show their bacterial past. They have two membranes, their own DNA, bacteria-like ribosomes, and they divide by pinching in two.

scenes.tts: Why did the partnership begin? The honest answer is that it is still debated.
scenes.visual: The merged cell centred, with two signposts branching away from it: 'hydrogen?' and 'oxygen?'. Label: 'Why did it start? Open question'.
scenes.narration: Why did the partnership begin? The honest answer is that it is still debated.

scenes.tts: The hydrogen hypothesis says the host lived on hydrogen. The bacterium gave off hydrogen as waste, so the two fed each other.
scenes.visual: Left signpost expands. The pink bacterium releases small white H2 bubbles; the amber host absorbs them. Arrows loop between the two: 'trading food'.
scenes.narration: The hydrogen hypothesis says the host lived on hydrogen. The bacterium gave off hydrogen as waste, so the two fed each other.

scenes.tts: The oxygen detoxification hypothesis says oxygen harmed the host. The bacterium consumed oxygen and shielded its partner.
scenes.visual: Right signpost expands. Red O2 molecules drift toward the host; the pink bacterium intercepts and consumes them, leaving a protected zone around the host.
scenes.narration: The oxygen detoxification hypothesis says oxygen harmed the host. The bacterium consumed oxygen and shielded its partner.

scenes.tts: Both ideas fit some evidence, and neither is proven. The first Asgard archaeon grown in a lab gives hydrogen to partner microbes. That is the reverse of the proposed host, but it shows such partnerships are real.
scenes.visual: Both signposts side by side, a balance scale between them, level. A small inset: a lab flask with a tangled Asgard archaeon releasing H2 bubbles that partner cells take up, labelled 'first cultured Asgard archaeon gives H2 to partners (Imachi et al., 2020)'.
scenes.narration: Both ideas fit some evidence, and neither is proven. The first Asgard archaeon grown in a lab gives hydrogen to partner microbes. That is the reverse of the proposed host, but it shows such partnerships are real.

scenes.tts: Oxygen changed the world the partners lived in. But eukaryote fossils appear long after the oxygen rise. How much oxygen drove their merger is still debated.
scenes.visual: The timeline again, the oxygenation band and the eukaryote zone separated by a visible gap.
scenes.narration: Oxygen changed the world the partners lived in. But eukaryote fossils appear long after the oxygen rise. How much oxygen drove their merger is still debated.

scenes.tts: Over time, the guest became an organelle. Many of its genes were lost, and others moved to the nucleus.
scenes.visual: Inside the merged cell, which already shows a nucleus. From the pink passenger's DNA, small gene blocks peel off: many fade away, and others fly into the nucleus. The passenger becomes a bean-shaped mitochondrion with folded cristae.
scenes.narration: Over time, the guest became an organelle. Many of its genes were lost, and others moved to the nucleus.

scenes.tts: But it kept a small genome of its own. Human mitochondrial DNA encodes just thirteen proteins, all for respiration and A T P synthesis.
scenes.visual: A small circular genome glows inside the mitochondrion. Thirteen small tiles spin off it and slot into the inner membrane among the respiratory complexes and ATP synthase. Label: 'human mtDNA: 13 proteins'.
scenes.narration: But it kept a small genome of its own. Human mitochondrial DNA encodes just thirteen proteins, all for respiration and A T P synthesis.

scenes.tts: One influential idea is that many mitochondria let eukaryotic cells afford larger genomes and more complex lives.
scenes.visual: Pull back: one cell now holds dozens of mitochondria, each glowing. The cell grows larger, sprouts internal membranes, and divides into a fan of descendants: an amoeba, a leaf cell, a fungal hypha, an animal cell.
scenes.narration: One influential idea is that many mitochondria let eukaryotic cells afford larger genomes and more complex lives.

scenes.visual: Hold on the fan of descendant cells, each glowing with mitochondria.

scenes.tts: So think back to the idea. Rust, poison and power are all ways of handling oxygen's electrons.
scenes.visual: A triptych: rust flakes settling (left), a crackling superoxide (centre), a calm water molecule at the end of a glowing chain (right). Yellow electrons link all three.
scenes.narration: So think back to the idea. Rust, poison and power are all ways of handling oxygen's electrons.

scenes.tts: In this lesson, follow electrons from N A D H down the chain to oxygen. Watch complex four hold oxygen until it is fully reduced to water.
scenes.visual: Zoom into a mitochondrion's inner membrane. NADH hands electrons to Complex I; they pass to ubiquinone (Q), then Complex III, then cytochrome c, then Complex IV, and on to O2. Complex II sits on a separate side branch, feeding electrons from succinate into Q and pumping no protons. Proton arrows cross the membrane only at Complexes I, III and IV. At Complex IV, already partly reduced, O2 binds at a heme–copper site; bound intermediates take electrons and protons in turn until two waters leave, and nothing partly reduced escapes.
scenes.narration: In this lesson, follow electrons from N A D H down the chain to oxygen. Watch complex four hold oxygen until it is fully reduced to water.

scenes.tts: That careful grip is the bargain. Every breath you take delivers oxygen to a chain inherited from that ancient guest.
scenes.visual: The camera pulls out from the membrane, through the mitochondrion, out of the cell, up through blue water, into a clear blue sky over a green coastline. The title THE OXYGEN BARGAIN fades in once more.
scenes.narration: That careful grip is the bargain. Every breath you take delivers oxygen to a chain inherited from that ancient guest.

scenes.visual: Hold on the blue sky and title, then fade to black.
